summary: Specifies a Forward Error Correction scheme using LDPC Staircase codes to protect media streams within the FECFRAME framework. Extra repair packets let a receiver rebuild lost ones without asking for retransmission. The codes are simple and efficient to encode and decode.

plainLanguage.summary: You send a puzzle with a few extra spare pieces. If some pieces get lost on the way, the spares let you finish the picture without asking for them again.

questions: how does forward error correction protect media streams
how does forward error correction work for streaming
subtitle: How to protect streaming media against packet loss by sending extra repair packets built with LDPC-Staircase codes.

tldr.problem: Real-time media streams lose packets, and asking the sender to resend them is slow or impossible for multicast and broadcast. FECFRAME needs a concrete code to plug in.
tldr.mechanism: Each application data unit becomes one source symbol, padded to a fixed length after a 3-byte prefix. The sender adds repair packets, each carrying one repair symbol. A receiver can rebuild lost source packets from what arrives.
tldr.outcome: It registers FEC Encoding ID 7 and reuses the core LDPC-Staircase code from RFC 5170. It is a Proposed Standard and has not been obsoleted or updated.

today: RFC 6816 is a Proposed Standard, and the unit metadata shows it has not been obsoleted or updated by another RFC. It builds on the core code in RFC 5170 and the framework in RFC 6363.

sections.title: What This Scheme Is For
sections.content:
Forward Error Correction (FEC) improves reliability by sending redundancy along with the data. RFC 6363 defines the FEC Framework (FECFRAME) for media delivery applications, for example real-time streaming over RTP. The framework needs an FEC scheme to do the actual coding, and this RFC supplies one based on LDPC-Staircase codes.

The RFC contrasts these codes with Reed-Solomon codes. Reed-Solomon is optimal in recovery power: any k of the n encoding symbols are enough. LDPC-Staircase needs a few symbols more than k, but the RFC says this excess is small in practice, and the codecs are much faster, by one or more orders of magnitude in software. Like Raptor and Reed-Solomon, the codes are systematic, meaning the source symbols are themselves part of the encoded output.

The core code and its pseudo-random number generator are inherited from RFC 5170. This document only adds what is specific to FECFRAME and replaces the formats and procedures that RFC 5170 defined for object delivery.
sections.plainLanguage: Streaming video can lose pieces on the way. Instead of asking for each lost piece again, the sender mixes in a few extra helper pieces ahead of time. This RFC says exactly how to make and label those helper pieces.

sections.title: Symbols, Blocks and Notation
sections.content:
An Application Data Unit (ADU) is the unit of source data handed to the transport layer, such as one RTP packet. In this scheme there is always exactly one source symbol per ADU. A source block holds k source symbols that are encoded together, and encoding produces n encoding symbols in total. Encoding symbols that are not source symbols are repair symbols.

The code rate is k/n. A rate close to 1 means few repair symbols. The RFC assumes a packet erasure channel, where each packet is either dropped or received intact.

Other notation: E is the encoding symbol length in bytes, N1 is the target number of 1s per column in the left side of the parity check matrix, and B is the number of ADUs in an ADU block.
sections.plainLanguage: Think of a box of numbered cards. Some cards are your real messages and some are extra backup cards. The code rate just says how many real cards there are compared with all the cards in the box.

sections.title: Building ADU Blocks and Source Blocks
sections.content:
The scheme has four hard restrictions: exactly one source symbol per ADU, exactly one repair symbol per FEC repair packet, exactly one source block per ADU block, and exactly one encoding symbol per group (G MUST equal 1).

The maximum block size is limited by the 16-bit Encoding Symbol ID field and the code rate. For a code rate of 1 the limit is 65536 symbols, for rates from 1/2 up to but not including 1 it is 32,768, and from 1/4 up to but not including 1/2 it is 16,384. A codec may add its own memory limit, and the real-time deadline adds another: with a maximum decoding latency l and an ADU covering duration d, a block may hold at most floor(l / d) ADUs. The RFC's example is d = 10 ms and l = 1 s, giving 100 ADUs. Bigger blocks mean longer waits before decoding can succeed.

Because every source symbol has the same length E, each ADU is wrapped into an ADU Information (ADUI): a 1-byte Flow ID, a 2-byte Length in big-endian order, the ADU itself, and zero padding up to exactly E bytes. If E is chosen per block (S = 0), it is the largest ADU in the block plus three. If E is fixed (S = 1), it must be at least that large, otherwise an error is returned. The prefix and padding are used in encoding but are never sent, so a receiver that rebuilds a lost ADUI can strip the padding and see which flow it belongs to.
sections.plainLanguage: To pack different-sized gifts into identical boxes, you put each one in a box and fill the empty space with tissue paper. You also stick a small label on it saying which flow it belongs to and how big it is. The tissue and label are never mailed, because the receiver can work them out.

sections.title: Configuration and Payload ID Formats
sections.content:
Sender and receiver must agree on the FEC Framework Configuration Information (FFCI). The FEC Encoding ID is 7. The scheme-specific part (FSSI) holds a 32-bit PRNG seed, the encoding symbol length E, the Strict flag S, and n1m3, an integer from 0 (default) to 7 so that N1 = n1m3 + 3. In SDP it is carried in the fssi parameter, for example fssi=seed:1234,E:1400,S:0,n1m3:0. As an opaque string it takes 7 octets: seed (32 bits), E (16 bits), S (1 bit), a 4-bit reserved field that MUST be zero, and n1m3 (3 bits).

An FEC source packet carries the ADU followed by an Explicit Source FEC Payload ID appended at the end. It has three 16-bit fields: Source Block Number (SBN), Encoding Symbol ID (ESI) and Source Block Length (k).

An FEC repair packet carries a Repair FEC Payload ID before its single repair symbol. It has four 16-bit fields: SBN, ESI, k and the number of encoding symbols n.
sections.plainLanguage: Every packet gets a small tag. The tag says which batch it belongs to, which numbered piece it is, and how big the batch is. Repair packets also say how many pieces there are in total.

sections.title: Numbering Blocks and Symbols
sections.content:
The SBN starts at 0 for the first block of the ADU flow and goes up by 1 for each new source block. It wraps to zero after 2^16 - 1 in long sessions. The ESI starts at 0 and is managed sequentially: values 0 to k - 1 identify source symbols, and values k to n - 1 identify repair symbols.

Because G must be 1, parts of RFC 5170 are not needed, notably its Section 5.6 on identifying the G symbols of an encoding symbol group.
sections.plainLanguage: Batches are numbered 0, 1, 2 and so on. Inside a batch, the real pieces come first and the spare pieces come after, all numbered in a row.

sections.title: Performance and Operating Advice
sections.content:
The RFC gives figures for k = 1024 source symbols, a code rate of 2/3 (512 repair symbols), N1 = 7 and G = 1. An ideal MDS code would tolerate a 33.33% channel loss rate. LDPC-Staircase needs an average overhead of 0.237% for a 0.5 probability of success, and an overhead of 1.46% (15 extra symbols) pushes the failure probability down to 8.2*10^-5. These results explain why the codes suit a single high bitrate flow, or several mid-rate flows protected together, with blocks of a few hundred symbols or more.

For smaller blocks recovery gets weaker, so the RFC recommends N1 of at least 7. With k = 256 the average overhead is 0.706%. For very small blocks of a few tens of symbols, Reed-Solomon or 2D parity codes may be more appropriate.

Decoding speed was measured with 1024-byte symbols. The RFC reports between 1.78 Gbps and 3.91 Gbps on an Intel Xeon 5120 workstation, and between 397 Mbps and 813 Mbps on a Samsung Galaxy SII smartphone. A good sending strategy is to send source packets first and in sequence, and repair packets in random order.
sections.plainLanguage: With a big pile of pieces, this trick needs only a tiny number of extra pieces to repair losses, and it works quickly even on a phone. With only a handful of pieces, other tricks work better.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC defers to the FEC Framework security analysis in RFC 6363 and adds points specific to LDPC-Staircase. If confidentiality matters, one of the RFC 6363 solutions is RECOMMENDED, with care about whether encryption happens before or after FEC. For corruption, integrity protection is RECOMMENDED on both source and repair packets.

An attacker who changes the FFCI can cause a denial of service. Changing the Encoding ID makes the receiver use a different scheme, changing n1m3 makes it use a different code, and a wrong E value makes symbol sizes incoherent. Flipping S from 0 to 1 can mislead a receiver when symbol sizes vary between blocks. Tampering with SBN, ESI, k or n in a payload ID can corrupt the block. The RFC therefore RECOMMENDS protecting FFCI integrity and the source and repair packets. IPsec/ESP remains the baseline mandatory-to-implement, but not mandatory-to-use, mechanism.
sections.plainLanguage: If a bad guy changes the instructions on the label, the receiver mixes up the puzzle. So the instructions and the pieces should be sealed so nobody can quietly change them.

sections.title: IANA Registration
sections.content: The RFC registers one value, 7, in the FEC Framework (FECFRAME) FEC Encoding IDs registry from RFC 6363. It stands for the Simple LDPC-Staircase FEC Scheme for Arbitrary Packet Flows, defined in Section 5 of the RFC.
sections.plainLanguage: It is like getting an official number on a list of codes, so everyone knows that 7 means this scheme.
